\chapter{RESULTS AND DISCUSSION}
\label{ch:results}

\section{Introduction}

This chapter reports the experimental results. It first establishes the dataset
characterisation and calibration, then reports the five segmentation methods
under the leave-one-specimen-out protocol of Section~\ref{sec:protocol}, then
tests the protocol itself against its naive alternative, and finally reports the
physical quantities the laboratory uses: bead count, areal density and the size
distribution in micrometres.

Three results are negative, and each is reported as prominently as the positive
ones. Mask R-CNN does not reach the provisional accuracy criterion set in
Section~\ref{sec:objectives}. The naive partitioning protocol does not overstate
performance on this dataset in the way the literature on small microscopy
datasets would lead one to expect. And none of the three preprocessing transforms
improves detection over the untransformed input, although one of them measurably
improves counting.

\section{Dataset Characterisation}

The descriptive analysis of the dataset is complete and is reported in
Chapter~\ref{ch:methodology}: 606 annotated beads across 11 micrographs of four
specimens, at three magnifications, with the pixel calibration of
Table~\ref{tab:calibration}.

The first objective of Section~\ref{sec:objectives} is met. The median equivalent
bead diameter is
7.92\,$\mu$m at $500\times$, 7.34\,$\mu$m at $1000\times$ and 6.75\,$\mu$m at
$3000\times$, an agreement of within 15\% against a stated criterion of 20\%. Since
the three magnifications image the same four specimens, this agreement is evidence
both that the scale calibration is correct and that the annotation is internally
consistent across magnifications -- an annotator who applied a different size
threshold at different magnifications would have broken it.

The residual downward trend with magnification is consistent with border clipping
rather than calibration error. At $3000\times$ the field is 94.8\,$\mu$m wide, so a
bead of 8\,$\mu$m occupies a much larger fraction of it and is correspondingly more
likely to intersect the image boundary and be excluded from annotation. Only 52 of
the 606 beads come from $3000\times$ micrographs, so this group is also the noisiest.

Pooled over all 11 micrographs and computed from rasterised masks rather than
polygon vertices, so as to be directly comparable with the predictions reported
later in this chapter, the manual median diameter is 7.97\,$\mu$m with an
interquartile range of 6.42 to 10.16\,$\mu$m.

\section{Experimental Setup}

\subsection{Training Configuration}

Table~\ref{tab:training_config} records the configuration used. Both models were
trained independently on each of the four folds from the same initialisation, on
a single NVIDIA T4.

\input{results/table_training_config}

\subsection{Justification of Training Hyperparameters}
\label{sec:training_config}

Four settings depart from what a default configuration would give, and each was
chosen from a measured property of the data rather than by search. This matters
for how the results should be read: no hyperparameter was tuned against
performance, so none of them can have been fitted to the test partitions.

\textbf{Anchor sizes: 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 pixels.} The torchvision default
begins at 32 pixels. The median bead is 14 pixels across at $500\times$, so under
the default the majority of objects at the lowest magnification would have no
anchor within a factor of two of their size, and the region proposal network would
be asked to regress a large correction for most of the dataset. The chosen ladder
brackets the observed range of 14 to 76 pixels, widened at both ends to cover the
random scaling applied during training.

\textbf{Detection cap: 400 per image.} The COCO default is 100. Micrograph Z6-1
contains 152 annotated beads, so the default would have truncated its output
before any threshold was applied. The failure would have been silent and would
have biased exactly the quantity this work measures. The cap is set high enough
that it never binds for the region-based detectors, and
Section~\ref{sec:yolo_results} reports the one method for which it does bind.

\textbf{Crop size $512 \times 512$ with scale jitter from 0.5 to 2.0.} A
leave-one-specimen-out training partition holds eight micrographs. Training on
whole images would therefore present eight distinct inputs; random crops draw a
different field of view each time. The scaling range is wider than is usual
because scale robustness across a sixfold range in apparent object size is the
central difficulty of this dataset rather than an incidental nuisance.

\textbf{Score threshold: selected per fold on training data.} The threshold
applied to each detector's output was chosen by maximising $F_1$ at an
intersection over union of 0.5 on each fold's own \emph{training} partition. For
Mask R-CNN the selected values were 0.55, 0.60, 0.60 and 0.60 on folds Z2, Z4, Z5
and Z6; for Faster R-CNN, 0.65, 0.65, 0.65 and 0.60; for YOLOv8, 0.15, 0.30, 0.15
and 0.15. This is the one free parameter of each learned pipeline, and selecting
it on test data would have inflated every number in this chapter. The U-Net's
probability threshold and minimum object area were chosen the same way, as were
the three parameters of the classical pipeline.

The gap between the two families is itself a finding rather than a detail. The
region-based detectors settle near 0.6 while YOLOv8 maximises training $F_1$ at
0.15, so the same criterion applied to the same folds selects an operating point
four times lower. That is a statement about how the two families calibrate their
confidence scores, not about their accuracy, and it means raw detection counts
are not comparable across the families without it.

The number of training iterations, 1500, was set by the available GPU budget
rather than by a convergence criterion. This is a limitation and is recorded as
one in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}: the reported figures are what this
configuration produces, not what the architecture is capable of.

\subsection{Computational Cost}
\label{sec:runtime}

Every method in this chapter was trained on a single NVIDIA T4 through Google
Colab. Four quantities are recorded per method: the median time per optimiser
step, the number of steps in an epoch, the resulting time per epoch, and the
total wall-clock time for one fold. Four folds are run per protocol, so a
complete cross-validation costs four times the last of these.

One definition has to be stated for those numbers to mean anything. Training
does not iterate a fixed set of images; it draws random $512 \times 512$ crops
on demand, so there is no natural epoch boundary. An epoch is therefore defined
here as one crop-equivalent pass over the eight training micrographs of a fold,
which at this crop size is 2.875 crops per micrograph. Reporting steps per epoch
alongside the step time makes the convention explicit rather than leaving the
reader to infer it, and the two together reconstruct any of the other figures.

Step times are medians rather than means, measured with the device synchronised
before the clock is read, and exclude the first step of each fold. Without the
synchronisation the measurement would record the time to enqueue the kernels
rather than to execute them, which on a GPU is a much smaller and quite
meaningless number; the first step is excluded separately because it carries
one-off allocation and kernel selection that recur nowhere else in the run.

% Emitted by make_tables.py only once at least one method has recorded timings.
% The sentence that cites the table lives inside the conditional as well, so that
% this file compiles with no undefined reference before the instrumented runs
% exist.
\IfFileExists{results/table_runtime.tex}{%
    Table~\ref{tab:runtime} gives these figures for every method.
    \input{results/table_runtime}%
}{}

Three comparisons in that table bear on conclusions drawn later in this chapter.

\textbf{The mask branch is nearly free.} Mask R-CNN costs 10.5 minutes per fold
against Faster R-CNN's 9.3: a 13\% premium for the branch that produces the
per-instance masks. Every mask-level quantity reported in this work -- the
Aggregated Jaccard Index, the merge and split rates, the size distribution in
micrometres -- is bought with that 13\%.

\textbf{YOLOv8 costs three times as much as Mask R-CNN.} At 32.0 minutes per fold
and 1.280 seconds per step against 0.405 at the same batch size, it is the most
expensive method measured. The difference is one of input size rather than of
architecture: its data pipeline expects a fixed image directory rather than the
crops drawn on demand by the torchvision models, so it was trained on whole
$1024$-pixel micrographs against their $512 \times 512$ crops. Its accuracy
results should not be read as though it had been given the smaller budget.

\textbf{The campaign as a whole is small.} Summed over every run reported in this
chapter -- five methods, three preprocessing variants and the random-split
control, four folds each -- training consumed 7.1 hours of T4 time. That figure
matters for reproducibility rather than for performance: the complete set of
results can be regenerated within a day on freely available hardware, which is a
property the design was chosen for rather than an accident of scale.

\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}

Every micrograph is scored exactly once, by the model of the fold that held its
specimen out. The eleven per-image results are therefore mutually independent in
the sense that no model contributed a score for a specimen it had seen, and
pooling them gives a single estimate over the whole dataset.

All five methods are evaluated by the same code, on the same predictions
format, against the same ground truth. This is not a convenience: a controlled
comparison is only meaningful if the differences between the methods come from the
methods. Each writes run-length-encoded masks in COCO results format, and the
evaluation module has no branch on which method produced them. The one exception
is declared rather than absorbed: Faster R-CNN predicts boxes and no masks, so its
average precision is computed at box overlap and it is absent from every
mask-level column. That is a different statement from scoring zero on them.

Metrics are computed at three levels, because a single number conceals the
failure modes that matter here. Average precision measures detection and
delineation jointly. The Aggregated Jaccard Index and Panoptic Quality measure
instance-level agreement, with Panoptic Quality decomposed into its recognition
and segmentation factors. Counting error, merge rate and split rate measure the
laboratory quantity directly. A method can score acceptably on the first and fail
completely on the third, and Section~\ref{sec:counting} shows that this is not a
hypothetical concern.

\subsection{Fold Composition}

\input{results/table_folds}

The folds are markedly unbalanced: specimen Z4 contributes only 63 beads across two
micrographs, while Z6 contributes 238 across three. Per-fold results are therefore
reported individually as well as averaged, since a mean over four folds of this
size is not a stable summary on its own.

One feature of that table looks like an error and is not. Fold Z2 shows 132
annotated beads against 144 predicted, and a counting error of $-1.4\%$. The count
columns are fold totals; the error column is the mean over the fold's three
micrographs of the per-micrograph signed error, and on Z2 those are $+29.6\%$,
$-13.7\%$ and $-20.0\%$. A fold whose micrographs err in opposite directions can
therefore carry a mean of either sign while its totals nearly agree. The
per-micrograph figure is the one reported throughout this chapter, because the
laboratory measures one micrograph at a time; the aggregate is reported separately
in Section~\ref{sec:counting}, where the gap between the two is itself the finding.

\section{Segmentation Results}

\subsection{Mask R-CNN}

\input{results/table_maskrcnn_results}

Mask R-CNN reaches $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.306 \pm 0.045$ averaged over the four
folds, with an Aggregated Jaccard Index of $0.320 \pm 0.055$ and a Panoptic
Quality of 0.343.

\textbf{This does not meet the provisional success criterion of
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} \geq 0.70$ stated in Section~\ref{sec:objectives}.} The third
objective is therefore not met at that threshold. The criterion was provisional
and awaits confirmation by the supervisor, but it is recorded here as stated
rather than adjusted after the fact to a value the result happens to clear.

The decomposition of Panoptic Quality is more informative than the headline
figure. Segmentation Quality -- the mean intersection over union of the beads
that were correctly matched -- is 0.693, while Recognition Quality is 0.495. The
model delineates well the beads it finds, and finds about half of them. Pooled
over all 11 held-out micrographs at an overlap of 0.5, it matches 305 of the 606
annotated beads and emits 331 detections that match nothing: a recall of 0.503 at
a precision of 0.480. The deficit is one of detection rather than of boundary
accuracy, and the gap between $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.306$ and
$\mathrm{AP}_{75} = 0.070$ says the same thing from the other direction:
performance falls away sharply as the required overlap tightens.

Per-fold results vary less than the counting results do. $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ ranges
from 0.260 on Z5 to 0.356 on Z4, and AJI from 0.267 on Z2 to 0.392 on Z4. Fold Z4
is the strongest on both, and rests on only 63 beads across two micrographs, so it
is also the least reliable of the four: its $3000\times$ micrograph carries four
annotated beads, so a single spurious detection on that frame is by itself a
counting error of 25 percentage points.

\subsection{U-Net Semantic Baseline}

The U-Net baseline reaches $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.152 \pm 0.042$, an AJI of 0.305
and a Panoptic Quality of 0.194. Its AJI is close to Mask R-CNN's, but its
Panoptic Quality is barely more than half, and the reason is visible in the
merge and split statistics.

The U-Net merges 48.7\% of ground-truth beads: nearly half of all annotated beads
end up inside a predicted region that has also swallowed at least one neighbour.
Its split rate is 0.0\%. It never fragments a bead and it very frequently fuses
adjacent ones, which is exactly the failure mode connected-component labelling
predicts. Two beads whose predicted regions touch by a single pixel become one
object, and no amount of semantic accuracy can undo that, because the information
distinguishing them was discarded when the instance identity was dropped.

The consequence for the measurement is direct and one-sided: the U-Net
under-counts by 44.2\% on average, and its signed error is $-44.2\%$ -- identical
to the absolute error, because every one of the four folds under-counts. A method
that merges cannot over-count, so its counting error carries a bias rather than
scatter, and no averaging over more micrographs will remove it. It is also the
most conservative method measured, returning 325 objects against 606 annotated at
a precision of 0.431 and a recall of only 0.231.

This is the clearest quantitative answer to the question of what instance-level
modelling buys on this data. It is not primarily mask accuracy -- the two methods'
AJI values differ by 0.015 -- but the ability to separate objects that touch.

\subsection{YOLOv8}
\label{sec:yolo_results}

YOLOv8 reaches $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.254 \pm 0.023$, an AJI of 0.254 and a
Panoptic Quality of 0.337. It is the second-best method on average precision and
the most stable across folds -- its between-fold standard deviation of 0.023 is
half Mask R-CNN's -- and it is by a wide margin the worst method on the quantity
this work exists to measure.

It reports 1223 objects against 606 annotated, a mean absolute counting error of
93.2\% and a mean signed error of $+84.9\%$. On specimen Z6 alone it returns 723
detections for 238 beads. That over-counting is not indiscriminate, which is what
makes it interesting: at an overlap of 0.5 it matches 422 of the 606 annotated
beads, a recall of 0.696 against Mask R-CNN's 0.503, and it has the highest
Recognition Quality of any method at 0.510. It genuinely finds more of the real
beads than any other method tested. It also emits 801 detections that match
nothing, for a precision of 0.345, and it splits 28.5\% of the beads it does find.

Two properties of the configuration explain the pattern rather than excusing it.
Its threshold was selected at 0.15 by the same training-fold $F_1$ criterion
applied to every other method, so the operating point is not a tuning artefact but
what that criterion selects for this model. And its 400-detection cap, chosen for
the region-based detectors, binds on Z6-1: it returns exactly 400 objects for 152
annotated beads, so the true over-count on that micrograph is at least what is
reported and possibly more.

The comparison with Mask R-CNN is therefore not a simple ranking. YOLOv8 has the
better recall and the worse precision; the better Recognition Quality and the
worse Segmentation Quality, 0.658 against 0.693; and a counting error more than
twice as large. For a laboratory that counts particles, the second of those
decides the matter. For a laboratory that wanted a candidate-generation stage
ahead of manual review, the first might.

\subsection{Faster R-CNN and the Value of the Mask Branch}

Faster R-CNN is included as the ablation of Mask R-CNN's mask branch: the same
backbone, the same feature pyramid, the same anchors, the same schedule, with the
mask head removed. It reaches $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.279 \pm 0.071$ at box overlap
and a box $F_1$ of 0.453, and it reports 619 objects against 606 annotated for a
mean absolute counting error of 45.9\%.

Its average precision is not comparable with the mask figures elsewhere in this
chapter and should not be read against them. A box has a systematically higher
overlap with its ground-truth box than a mask has with its ground-truth mask, for
objects of this shape, so the two quantities differ in what they measure and not
merely in magnitude. The comparison the ablation does support is on the counting
endpoint, which is defined identically for both: 45.9\% for the detector against
41.1\% for the same architecture with the mask branch attached, at a training cost
13\% lower.

The honest reading of that pair is that on counting alone the mask branch buys
little -- under five percentage points, well inside the fold-to-fold spread of
either method. What it buys is everything else: without it there is no Aggregated
Jaccard Index, no merge or split rate, and no size distribution in micrometres,
because there is no object boundary to measure. Since the size distribution is one
of the two quantities the laboratory asked for, the mask branch is not optional
here even though its effect on the count is small.

\subsection{Classical Baseline}

The Otsu-plus-watershed pipeline fails on this data. It reaches
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.001$, an AJI of 0.067 and a Panoptic Quality of 0.013, and
over-counts by 574\% on average: 2205 objects reported against 606 annotated. At
an overlap of 0.5 it matches 28 beads out of 606, a recall of 0.046 at a precision
of 0.013.

The failure has a measurable cause rather than being an artefact of poor tuning.
The contrast the method depends on is very weak: measured over the annotated
regions, the mean grey level inside a bead is 98 against 116 outside on Z2-1, 115
against 135 on Z5-2, and 81 against 104 on Z6-4 -- a separation of roughly 20 grey
levels in an image whose fibre network produces edges of comparable strength
everywhere. A global Otsu threshold therefore returns a speckled foreground whose
area bears little relation to the beads, and the distance-transform watershed then
partitions that speckle into hundreds of fragments.

Figure~\ref{fig:contrast} shows why no choice of threshold could have rescued the
method. The grey-level distributions inside and outside the beads are not merely
close; they overlap along almost their entire range. Any global threshold that
captured most bead pixels would also capture a large share of the background, and
one that excluded the background would exclude most of the beads. The failure is a
property of the images, not of the parameter search.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_contrast.pdf}
    \caption{Grey-level distributions inside and outside the annotated beads, for
    one micrograph at each magnification. The means differ by about 20 levels
    while the distributions overlap almost entirely, which is the condition under
    which global thresholding cannot work.}
    \label{fig:contrast}
\end{figure}

The parameters were tuned by grid search on each fold's training partition over
morphological kernel size, minimum accepted object area in $\mu$m$^2$ and marker
suppression distance. The grid brackets the median annotated bead area of about
38\,$\mu$m$^2$ from well below to well above, and the selected optimum falls in
the interior of the grid for all four folds, so the result is not an artefact of
too narrow a search.

Its Segmentation Quality of 0.489 against a Recognition Quality of 0.021 completes
the picture: on the rare occasion it matches a bead, the mask is not unreasonable;
it almost never matches one.

\subsection{Method Comparison}
\label{sec:comparison}

\input{results/table_method_comparison}

Mask R-CNN leads on every mask-level metric measured -- average precision,
Aggregated Jaccard Index, counting error -- and the classical pipeline is last on
every one of them. The fourth objective of Section~\ref{sec:objectives} is met.
The ordering in between depends on which metric is asked for, and that dependence
is a result rather than an inconvenience: YOLOv8 beats the U-Net on average
precision, 0.254 against 0.152, and loses to it on counting error, 93.2\% against
44.2\%.

The methods fail in four distinguishable ways, and the counting column separates
them more clearly than the accuracy columns do.

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{The classical pipeline fragments texture into objects.} It
    over-counts by a factor of seven, with a signed error of $+574\%$.

    \item \textbf{The U-Net fuses neighbours.} It under-counts by 44\%, merges
    48.7\% of beads and splits none, and its error is entirely one-signed.

    \item \textbf{YOLOv8 detects freely and fragments what it detects.} It
    over-counts by 93\%, with the highest recall and the highest split rate,
    28.5\%, of any method.

    \item \textbf{Mask R-CNN errs in both directions.} Its mean absolute counting
    error of 41.1\% is the lowest of the four, and its mean signed error is
    $+20.9\%$: half its absolute error cancels between micrographs that over- and
    under-count, against a U-Net whose error cancels not at all.
\end{itemize}

That last distinction matters for the application and is discussed further in
Section~\ref{sec:counting}, because a method whose errors partly cancel across
specimens is useful for a population estimate in a way that a biased method is
not, while still being unreliable for any single micrograph.

Table~\ref{tab:counting} restates the comparison on the counting endpoint alone.
It is separated from Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} because counting error and
the raw count are the only quantities defined identically for a method that
predicts masks and one that predicts only boxes, so it is the one place where
every method can be listed without qualification. Where a row is marked
\emph{box}, its average precision is computed on bounding boxes rather than
masks, and the two are not interchangeable.

\input{results/table_counting}

Table~\ref{tab:ap_bands} decomposes average precision by object size. This
matters more here than the pooled figure suggests: 82.8\% of the annotated
particles fall in COCO's small band and 1.2\% in its large band
(Section~\ref{sec:small_objects}), so the pooled AP is close to an average over a
single band while appearing to describe three. $\mathrm{AP}_S$ is the column that
characterises this dataset, and it is the column that should be compared against
the small-object literature of Table~\ref{tab:coco_size} rather than the pooled
COCO figures usually quoted.

\input{results/table_ap_bands}

Two features of that table are worth stating. First, every learned method scores
higher on the medium and large bands than on the small one, which is the expected
direction and is the same effect Section~\ref{sec:magnification} measures against
magnification. Second, the large-band column rests on the thinnest evidence in the
chapter: 1.2\% of the annotations are large, fold Z4 contains none at all, and the
column is therefore averaged over three folds rather than four. YOLOv8's
$\mathrm{AP}_L$ of 0.040 against Faster R-CNN's 0.182 is a difference between two
numbers each computed from a handful of objects, and nothing in this work should
be concluded from it.

\subsection{Effect of Input Preprocessing}
\label{sec:preprocessing_results}

The four preprocessing variants of Section~\ref{sec:preprocessing_method} can be
characterised before any model is trained, by measuring on the annotations
themselves what contrast each one leaves available. Table~\ref{tab:contrast}
reports two quantities per variant: the mean grey-level separation between
particle and mat, and that separation divided by the standard deviation of the
background. The second is the one that matters. A transform that widens the gap
while widening the spread by more has not made the particles easier to find, and
reporting only the first would rank such a transform highest.

\begin{table}[htbp]
    \centering
    \caption{Particle-to-mat contrast under each preprocessing variant, measured
    over all 606 annotated particles in the 11 micrographs before any training.
    $\Delta$ is the mean grey level outside a particle minus the mean inside;
    $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of the background. $\Delta/\sigma$ is the
    contrast a filter or a threshold actually has to work with.}
    \label{tab:contrast}
    \begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
        \toprule
        Preprocessing & $\Delta$ (grey levels) & $\sigma$ & $\Delta/\sigma$ &
        Change \\
        \midrule
        None (baseline)        & 18.0 & 33.2 & 0.550 & ---      \\
        Median filter, $3\times3$ & 18.3 & 30.5 & 0.612 & $+11\%$ \\
        Background subtraction & 20.3 & 34.9 & 0.593 & $+8\%$  \\
        CLAHE                  & 23.1 & 62.5 & 0.372 & $-32\%$ \\
        \bottomrule
    \end{tabular}
\end{table}

CLAHE is the instructive case. It produces the widest raw separation of the four,
23.1 grey levels against the baseline's 18.0, and on that number alone would be
the obvious choice. It also nearly doubles the background standard deviation,
from 33.2 to 62.5, because the transform cannot distinguish a particle from the
fibre texture surrounding it and amplifies both. The usable contrast falls by
almost a third. Figure~\ref{fig:preprocessing} shows this directly: in the CLAHE
panel the fibres are as strongly modulated as the particle.

The other two transforms produce modest gains. The median filter improves
$\Delta/\sigma$ by 11\% by reducing the background spread rather than by
increasing the separation, which is the expected behaviour of a denoising filter
on a signal it does not otherwise disturb. Background subtraction improves it by
8\%, and its raw separation rises to 20.3, indicating that some of the measured
particle-to-mat difference in the untransformed images is attributable to
illumination gradient rather than to the particles.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_preprocessing.pdf}
    \caption{One region of Z6-4 under each preprocessing variant, with the
    contrast each yields over the whole dataset. The CLAHE panel is the reason
    the normalised measure is reported rather than the raw separation: the
    particle is more strongly contrasted than in the baseline, and so is every
    fibre around it.}
    \label{fig:preprocessing}
\end{figure}

Two cautions attach to Table~\ref{tab:contrast}. It measures contrast, not
accuracy, and a convolutional detector is not a threshold: it can exploit texture
and shape that this statistic ignores, so a variant may help or harm detection in
ways the table does not predict. And the models here are initialised from weights
trained on natural images, so a transform that moves the intensity statistics far
from that distribution may cost more than the contrast it buys. The measured
contrast is a prior on where to look, not a substitute for the comparison.

% The accuracy comparison appears here once the preprocessing runs exist;
% make_tables.py emits table_preprocessing.tex only when at least two variants
% have been evaluated, so this file compiles either way.
\IfFileExists{results/table_preprocessing.tex}{%
    \input{results/table_preprocessing}%
}{}

That comparison has now been run, and it is worth stating plainly what it found:
\textbf{no transform improves detection over the untransformed input.} Mask R-CNN
scores $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.306$ on the raw micrographs, against 0.289 with the
median filter, 0.263 with background subtraction and 0.262 with CLAHE. The
ordering on $\mathrm{AP}_S$, the band that describes this dataset, is the same.
Architecture, schedule, folds and threshold-selection rule were identical across
the four rows, so the differences are attributable to the input transform alone.

The contrast statistic of Table~\ref{tab:contrast} therefore succeeded at one of
its two jobs. It correctly identified the harmful transform: CLAHE loses a third
of the usable contrast and is last or joint-last on every accuracy column. It
failed to identify a beneficial one, having predicted gains of 11\% and 8\% for
the median filter and background subtraction, both of which cost detection
accuracy instead. The caution stated above -- that a detector is not a threshold,
and that a transform which moves intensity statistics away from the pretrained
distribution can cost more than the contrast it buys -- is the likeliest
explanation, and it is a caution recorded before the runs rather than after them.

One row of the table points the other way, and it happens to be the row the
laboratory cares about most. Background subtraction gives the lowest counting
error of the four variants, 31.3\% against the baseline's 41.1\%, while losing
0.043 of $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$. It does so by making fewer of both kinds of instance
error: its merge rate is 26.4\% against 30.0\% and its split rate 11.6\% against
20.3\%, the lowest split rate of any Mask R-CNN variant. Its Panoptic Quality,
0.344, is indistinguishable from the baseline's 0.343. The median filter shows the
same effect more weakly, at 36.4\%.

The reading this supports is narrow and should not be widened. Removing the
illumination gradient does not help the detector find beads, and on this evidence
slightly hinders it; what it does is make the boundaries it draws less likely to
fragment, which is what the counting endpoint rewards. A pipeline optimised for
average precision would use the raw input, and a pipeline optimised for counting
would use background subtraction. These runs cannot say which difference would
survive a second seed, and Section~\ref{sec:reliability} explains why.

\subsection{Qualitative Examples}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_qualitative.pdf}
    \caption{The four mask-predicting methods on two held-out micrographs, Z6-1
    at $500\times$ and Z2-2 at $1000\times$. Every panel is produced by a model
    that never saw that specimen. Red outlines are the manual annotation, blue
    the prediction. Faster R-CNN is absent because it predicts no masks to
    outline.}
    \label{fig:qualitative}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:qualitative} shows the mask-predicting methods on two held-out
micrographs, and each of the numerical findings above has a visible counterpart
in it.

On Z6-1 the annotator marked 152 beads. The classical pipeline returns 329
regions that tile the frame more or less irrespective of where the beads are:
its outlines follow the fibre texture, which is the visual form of an
$\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ of 0.001. The U-Net returns 77 regions, half the true count,
and they are visibly larger than individual beads because adjacent beads have
been absorbed into single components --- the 48.7\% merge rate made visible.
YOLOv8 returns 400, hitting the detection cap, with many small outlines
subdividing single annotated beads. Mask R-CNN returns 131 regions that
correspond recognisably to individual beads, and its errors are of a different
kind: beads missed entirely rather than beads fused or fragmented.

On Z2-2, where the annotator marked 51 beads, the same pattern holds at a
different scale. The classical pipeline returns 311 regions; the U-Net 31 and
Mask R-CNN 44, both under-counting, but the U-Net's regions again span
neighbouring beads while Mask R-CNN's do not; YOLOv8 returns 67, over-counting
where the other two under-count.

The panels also show what the summary statistics cannot: the beads themselves are
low-contrast objects embedded in a dense fibre network, and in several places the
distinction between a bead and a locally thickened fibre crossing is genuinely
ambiguous to the eye. This is the limitation recorded in
Section~\ref{sec:limitations} concerning the single annotation class, and it
places an unknown ceiling on what any model can be expected to achieve against
this ground truth.

\section{The Cost of a Naive Split}
\label{sec:leakage}

\input{results/table_leakage}

This is a negative result and it is reported as measured.

Evaluating the same model under a random split over the 11 micrographs, with fold
sizes identical to the specimen-wise protocol, gives
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.303$ against 0.306 for leave-one-specimen-out -- a
difference of $-0.003$, against a between-fold standard deviation of 0.045 for the
specimen-wise protocol. AJI differs by $-0.007$ and mean absolute counting error
by 3.7 percentage points. Every one of those differences favours the specimen-wise
protocol, which is the opposite of the direction a leak would produce. On this
dataset, the naive protocol does not overstate performance.

The second objective of Section~\ref{sec:objectives} asked for a demonstration
that the naive alternative overstates performance, and that demonstration did not
materialise. The protocol remains the correct one to use, but on the strength of
structural argument rather than of measured inflation, and the distinction should
be stated rather than blurred.

Three factors plausibly explain the absence of a gap, and the first is the most
likely.

\textbf{The leak that mattered had already been removed.} The 132 pre-computed
augmented copies were discarded before any partitioning, as described in
Section~\ref{sec:supplied_aug}. Those copies are near-duplicates of their
originals, and allowing them to cross a partition boundary would put a
transformed version of a test image directly into training. The remaining
dependence between two micrographs of the same specimen at different
magnifications is far weaker: they show different fields of view at different
scales, and share only the specimen's general morphology.

\textbf{There is little headroom to inflate.} A protocol can only flatter a model
that is capable of memorising. At $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.31$ and a Recognition
Quality of 0.49, this model is under-fitting the task rather than memorising
specimens, and there is correspondingly little for a leak to exploit.

\textbf{With 11 images, both protocols are noisy.} The random split's folds range
from $\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.199$ to 0.423, a spread of 0.224, against 0.260 to
0.356 for the specimen-wise folds, a spread of 0.096. The random protocol did not
give a higher mean, but it gave one whose fold-to-fold spread is 2.3 times as wide. That is a reason to prefer the specimen-wise protocol independent of any
bias argument: it is the more stable estimator, and on four folds stability is
worth more than it would be on forty.

The honest conclusion is that on this dataset the choice of protocol changes the
answer very little, and that the argument for partitioning by specimen rests on
what could happen with a stronger model and on estimator variance, not on a
measured gap in these runs.

\section{Behaviour Across Magnification}
\label{sec:magnification}

\input{results/table_magnification}

Detection improves monotonically with magnification, which is the opposite of
what the sample sizes alone would predict. The $3000\times$ group is the smallest
in the dataset -- 52 beads across four micrographs, against 325 at $500\times$ --
and it is nonetheless the group on which the model detects best, at
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.404$ and AJI 0.338 against 0.237 and 0.252 at $500\times$.

Object size, not sample size, is the binding constraint. The median bead is 14
pixels across at $500\times$ and 76 at $3000\times$. At 14 pixels a bead spans
roughly the receptive field of the finest pyramid level and is only a few pixels
larger than the smallest anchor, and the boundary of such an object is decided by
a handful of pixels; at 76 pixels it is a comfortably resolved object. The
feature pyramid and the rescaled anchors were introduced to handle this sixfold
range, and Table~\ref{tab:magnification} shows that they narrow the gap without
closing it.

Counting runs the other way, and the two trends have to be read together. The
absolute counting error is worst at $3000\times$, 55.9\% against 32.1\% at
$500\times$, and this is an arithmetic property of the field of view rather than a
contradiction of the detection result. A $3000\times$ micrograph carries 13
annotated beads on average and as few as four; one spurious detection on a
four-bead frame is a 25\% error, while one spurious detection on the 152-bead
Z6-1 is 0.7\%. The model sees each bead more clearly at high magnification and
reports the count of a much smaller sample.

The practical consequence for the laboratory follows from the combination rather
than from either trend alone. High magnification gives more reliable per-bead
measurements -- better boundaries, and therefore a better size distribution -- and
a less reliable count, because it counts fewer objects over a smaller field. Low
magnification gives the more reliable count and the coarser boundaries. If both
quantities are wanted from one setting, $1000\times$ is the compromise these
results support: it is within 0.060 of the best $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ and within
3.2 percentage points of the best counting error, whereas each of the extremes is
clearly worse on one of the two.

The caveat is that 52 beads is a small sample, and the $3000\times$ figures should
be read as indicative rather than settled.

\section{Physical Quantification}

\subsection{Bead Count and Areal Density}
\label{sec:counting}

Summed over all 11 held-out micrographs, Mask R-CNN reports 636 beads against 606
annotated, an aggregate excess of 5.0\%. That figure is far more favourable than
the method deserves, because it is the sum of errors that largely cancel.

Per specimen the mean signed error runs from $-1.4\%$ on Z2 to $+54.8\%$ on Z6,
and per micrograph from $-52.9\%$ on Z5-1 to $+103.2\%$ on Z6-2. The mean absolute
error per fold is 41.1\% while the mean signed error is $+20.9\%$. A single
micrograph is therefore not a reliable measurement, and an aggregate over many
micrographs is considerably better than any one of them -- 5.0\% against 41.1\% is
a factor of eight, and none of that improvement comes from the model being right.

Figure~\ref{fig:counting} plots the two counts against each other. Five of the
eleven micrographs fall within 25\% of the annotated count, and the two largest
errors lie on opposite sides: Z5-1 is under-counted by half, and Z6-2 is nearly
doubled. Both are among the more densely populated micrographs, which is where a
merge or a spurious split costs most.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.78\textwidth]{figures/fig_counting.pdf}
    \caption{Predicted against annotated bead count for each held-out micrograph,
    with marker shape indicating magnification. Points on the diagonal agree
    exactly. The aggregate excess of 5.0\% is the net effect of errors that run in
    both directions and largely cancel.}
    \label{fig:counting}
\end{figure}

Areal density inherits this behaviour directly, since it is the count divided by a
known physical area. On Z2-1 the model reports 395 beads\,mm$^{-2}$ against 305
measured manually; on Z5-1 it reports 206 against 438; on Z6-2, 2166 against 1066.
The fifth objective of Section~\ref{sec:objectives} is met in the sense that these
quantities are reported and compared, but the comparison does not support using
the pipeline as a drop-in replacement for manual counting on a single field.

\subsection{Size Distribution Agreement}

\input{results/table_physical}

Mask R-CNN's predicted median diameter is 7.51\,$\mu$m against 7.97\,$\mu$m
measured manually, a difference of 5.8\%, with an interquartile range of 5.61 to
8.94\,$\mu$m against 6.42 to 10.16\,$\mu$m. The predicted distribution is narrower
and smaller, consistent with a detector that misses the beads hardest to
delineate and trims the boundaries of those it keeps.

All four two-sample Kolmogorov--Smirnov tests reject the hypothesis that the
predicted and manual distributions are the same. Three of them reject at
$p < 10^{-3}$; YOLOv8's rejects only at $p = 0.02$. That rejection should not be
over-read. With hundreds of samples on each side the test is sensitive to
differences far smaller than those that would matter for process optimisation,
and statistical significance here is not the same as practical disagreement: a
5.8\% error in median bead diameter is smaller than the 15\% spread the same
annotation shows across magnifications.

Figure~\ref{fig:size_agreement} shows why the summary statistics should be read
alongside the distributions. Mask R-CNN tracks the manual distribution closely
through its bulk and falls short in the tail above roughly 15\,$\mu$m.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{figures/fig_size_agreement.pdf}
    \caption{Predicted against manual bead size distributions, pooled over all
    11 held-out micrographs.}
    \label{fig:size_agreement}
\end{figure}

Two rows of Table~\ref{tab:physical} are a warning rather than a finding, and
together they make the point more sharply than either does alone. YOLOv8 has the
\emph{lowest} Kolmogorov--Smirnov statistic of the four methods, $D = 0.075$, and
the classical pipeline the second lowest, $D = 0.105$ -- and these are the two
methods that over-count by 93\% and 574\% respectively. Both achieve their
agreement by reporting far more objects than exist, whose sizes happen to span a
similar range to the real beads. Mask R-CNN, the best method by every other
measure in this chapter, has a worse $D$ than both.

Distributional agreement alone is therefore not a sufficient criterion. A method
can reproduce the size distribution of a population it has substantially failed to
identify, and this is exactly why counting error and instance-level metrics are
reported alongside it rather than in its place. Had this work reported only the
size distribution -- which is one of the two quantities the laboratory asked for
-- it would have ranked the two worst methods first.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{Key Findings}

\textbf{Instance segmentation is the right formulation, and the reason is
separation rather than accuracy.} Mask R-CNN and the U-Net differ by 0.015 in
AJI but by 0.149 in Panoptic Quality and by 18.7 percentage points in merge rate.
What the instance formulation buys on this data is the ability to keep touching
beads apart. That the annotation itself contains 8.8\% overlapping bead pixels
confirms that touching beads are common rather than exceptional here.

\textbf{The instance formulation trades one error for another rather than
eliminating error.} The U-Net merges 48.7\% of beads and splits none; Mask R-CNN
merges 30.0\% and splits 20.3\%; YOLOv8 merges 34.5\% and splits 28.5\%. Nothing
tested here separates touching beads without also fragmenting some of them, and
the counting error of every method is dominated by whichever of the two it does
more of.

\textbf{Classical thresholding is not a viable baseline for this modality.} At
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.001$ it is not merely worse than the learned methods but
unusable, and the measured bead-to-background separation of about 20 grey levels
explains why.

\textbf{The absolute performance is not yet sufficient for unattended use.} An
$\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ of 0.306 and a per-fold counting error of 41.1\% do not support
replacing a human operator on a single micrograph. What the pipeline can support
is triage and aggregate estimation, where the aggregate error over eleven
micrographs is 5.0\%.

\textbf{Small objects, not scarce labels, are the binding constraint on
detection.} Detection is best where the data are scarcest and the objects are
largest. Counting runs the other way, for a reason that is arithmetic rather than
architectural.

\textbf{Preprocessing did not improve detection, and one variant improved
counting.} No transform beat the raw input on $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$; background
subtraction cut counting error from 41.1\% to 31.3\% by halving the split rate.
The contrast measured on the annotations before training predicted the harmful
transform correctly and the helpful ones wrongly.

\textbf{The specimen-wise protocol did not change the headline number, but it
more than halved the fold-to-fold spread.} That is a weaker claim than the one anticipated in
Section~\ref{sec:objectives}, and it is the one the data support.

\subsection{Comparison with the Literature}

Direct numerical comparison with published work is not possible, because no public
benchmark for bead defects in electrospun mats exists and the AP values reported
here are specific to this annotation and this protocol. Three qualitative
comparisons can be made.

The merge behaviour of semantic segmentation with connected-component
post-processing is well documented in the nuclei segmentation literature, and is
the motivation for the boundary-aware and shape-prior methods of
Schmidt et al.\ \cite{schmidt2018stardist} and Stringer et al.\
\cite{stringer2021cellpose} and for the weighted-boundary loss of the original
U-Net \cite{ronneberger2015unet, falk2019unet}. The 48.7\% merge rate measured
here is a direct instance of that effect, and its magnitude is a consequence of
how frequently beads touch in these micrographs.

The difficulty of small objects for region-based detectors is likewise a known
property of the architecture rather than of this dataset, and is what the feature
pyramid \cite{lin2017feature} was introduced to address. The results of
Table~\ref{tab:ap_bands} and Table~\ref{tab:magnification} are consistent with the
general finding that performance degrades with object size in pixels, and the
one-stage detector's weakness on small objects reported for the YOLO family
\cite{redmon2016yolo, lin2020focal} appears here as an $\mathrm{AP}_S$ of 0.091
against Mask R-CNN's 0.116.

The absolute values reported here are well below those typically reported on
nuclei benchmarks such as the dataset of Kumar et al.\ \cite{kumar2017dataset}.
The relevant difference is training set size: those results rest on tens of
thousands of annotated objects, against 606 here from four specimens, of which
roughly three-quarters are available for training in any fold.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

The limitations below follow from the dataset and from the experimental design.

\textbf{Four specimens.} The strongest claim this dataset can support is
generalisation across four specimens of what appears to be one material system. It
cannot establish generalisation to a different polymer, a different solvent or a
different instrument.

\textbf{Fifty-two beads at $3000\times$.} The highest magnification is represented by
only 52 annotated objects, so the per-magnification result for $3000\times$ --
which is also the most striking finding of
Section~\ref{sec:magnification} -- rests on a small sample
and should be read as indicative.

\textbf{One annotator.} All 606 annotations come from a single source, so
annotator bias cannot be distinguished from ground truth, and no inter-annotator
agreement can be reported. This matters more than usual here, because at
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.306$ it is not known how much of the shortfall is model
error and how much is disagreement that a second annotator would also show.
% TODO(supervisor): if a subset can be re-annotated by a second person, this
% limitation can be converted into a measurement instead. See question D4.

\textbf{Single class.} The annotation does not distinguish beads from locally
thickened fibre segments, so the boundary between the two is defined implicitly by
the annotator's judgement rather than by a stated criterion. Several of the
model's false positives on visual inspection are objects of this ambiguous kind.

\textbf{No hyperparameter search.} Every model was trained once, with the
configuration of Table~\ref{tab:training_config}, for 1500 iterations. The
reported figures are what that configuration produces, not the best achievable,
and the training budget was set by the available GPU time rather than by
convergence.

\textbf{YOLOv8 was not given a matched input budget.} It was trained on whole
$1024$-pixel micrographs where the region-based models saw $512 \times 512$ crops,
because its data pipeline expects a fixed image directory. Its accuracy figures
are therefore not a like-for-like architectural comparison, and its threefold
training cost is largely a consequence of that difference.

\textbf{The detection cap binds for YOLOv8 on one micrograph.} It returns exactly
400 objects on Z6-1, so its over-count there, and hence its pooled counting error,
is a lower bound rather than a measurement.

\subsection{Reliability of the Reported Numbers}
\label{sec:reliability}

Each configuration was run \emph{once}, with a fixed seed of 0. No seed was
varied and no configuration was repeated, so every figure in this chapter is a
single-run point estimate and none of the reported standard deviations is a
measure of run-to-run variability. They are between-fold spreads over four folds,
which is a different and weaker quantity: it describes how much the result
depends on which specimen was held out, not how much it would move if the same
experiment were repeated.

With four folds, a standard deviation is itself estimated from four numbers and
should not be treated as a confidence interval. Varoquaux
\cite{varoquaux2018crossvalidation} shows that cross-validated estimates from small
samples carry error bars far wider than is usually assumed, and that differences
well below those error bars are routinely reported as findings. Two comparisons in
this chapter are the most exposed to that. The protocol comparison of
Section~\ref{sec:leakage} turns on a difference of 0.003 in $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$,
which is a fifteenth of the between-fold standard deviation, so the correct reading
is that no difference was detected, not that the two protocols were shown to be
equivalent. The preprocessing comparison of
Section~\ref{sec:preprocessing_results} turns on differences of 0.017 to 0.044 in
$\mathrm{AP}_{50}$, against a between-fold standard deviation of 0.045 for the
baseline: the direction is consistent across the three variants, which is some
evidence, but no single pairwise difference there is resolved by these runs.

What can be stated robustly is the ranking of the classical pipeline against the
learned methods, which is consistent across every metric and every fold; the
direction and magnitude of the merge, split and counting biases, which are large
and systematically signed; and the gap between per-micrograph and aggregate
counting error, which is a factor of eight. What cannot be stated robustly is any
small difference between two similar numbers, including the ordering of Mask R-CNN
against YOLOv8 on average precision.

\section{Summary}

Mask R-CNN outperforms the alternatives on every mask-level metric, reaching
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.306 \pm 0.045$, AJI $0.320 \pm 0.055$ and a mean absolute
counting error of 41.1\% under leave-one-specimen-out cross-validation. It does
not reach the provisional criterion of $\mathrm{AP}_{50} \geq 0.70$.

The U-Net baseline merges 48.7\% of beads and under-counts by 44\% with an error
that never changes sign, which identifies object separation rather than mask
accuracy as what the instance formulation contributes. YOLOv8 finds more of the
real beads than any other method, at a recall of 0.696, and reports twice as many
objects as exist. Faster R-CNN shows that removing the mask branch costs about
five percentage points of counting error and all of the mask-level measurements,
for 13\% less training time. The classical pipeline fails outright, at
$\mathrm{AP}_{50} = 0.001$, for a reason measurable in the images themselves.

Detection improves with magnification despite the smallest sample being at the
highest magnification, identifying object size in pixels as the binding
constraint; counting degrades with magnification, for the arithmetic reason that
a smaller field holds fewer beads. No preprocessing variant improved detection
over the raw input, and background subtraction reduced counting error from 41.1\%
to 31.3\%. The naive partitioning protocol did not overstate performance, though
it produced a fold-to-fold spread 2.3 times as wide. Predicted bead diameters
agree with the manual measurement to 5.8\% in the median, while counting remains
too variable per micrograph -- 41.1\% against an aggregate 5.0\% over eleven
micrographs -- for unattended use.
